name: Porcelain veneers
lead: Porcelain veneers are thin, custom-made shells, usually of porcelain or glass-ceramic, bonded to the front of teeth to change their colour, shape, size or spacing [1][2]. For appearance, the payoff is a whiter, more even and better-proportioned smile: veneers can mask stains, close gaps, lengthen worn teeth and give a uniform look across the upper arch, which is why multiple veneers are a common smile-makeover approach [1]. They are made indirectly by a dental technician, unlike composite veneers, which can be built directly in the mouth [1].

A 2016 meta-analysis of clinical trials on feldspathic porcelain and glass-ceramic laminate veneers examined survival and complications including debonding and fracture [3], and a ten-year prospective trial followed 87 veneers in 25 patients [4]. A 2018 review describes them as showing excellent aesthetic results and predictable longevity [12]. Wikipedia reports lifespans of 10 to 30 years with modern bonding, with reasons for replacement including chipping, discoloration and decay, and notes that preparation can remove tooth structure [1].

Veneers are among the best-documented cosmetic dental treatments, with decades of clinical follow-up, and they are also one of the most discussed in debates about cost, overuse and tooth reduction [1][6].
infobox: Some enamel removal; thin 'no-prep' types exist [1]

paras: Wikipedia distinguishes laminate veneers, which cover only the front surface of a tooth, from full veneer crowns that cover all surfaces [1]. Porcelain veneers are made only indirectly and are described as more durable and less stain-prone than composite, which can be placed directly in the mouth or built in a lab and has a reported lifespan of about four years [1]. A 2025 review covers direct composite veneers for smile rehabilitation [17].

Materials include feldspathic and leucite-reinforced ceramics, lithium disilicate and zirconia [1]. A 2018 update describes new glass-ceramics with strength and optical properties suited to veneers and crowns, and a randomized trial has compared ultra-translucent multilayered zirconia with lithium disilicate laminates at 18 months [11][15]. Preparation designs are called window, feather, bevel and incisal overlap; a 2018 review found clinician preference decisive, with incisal overlap appearing most predictable [1][12].

A 2012 system called the Nankali Veneer Classification, described in Wikipedia, sorts veneers by how much of the labial surface they cover, whether they involve the contact points between teeth, whether they are made directly or indirectly, and by material.[1] Wikipedia notes that acrylic is no longer used for quality work.[1]

Wikipedia credits California dentist Charles Pincus with making veneers for a film shoot in 1928 and acrylic versions retained with denture adhesive in 1937, Michael Buonocore's enamel-etching work in 1959 as the basis for bonding, and Simonsen and Calamia in 1982-83 with showing porcelain could be etched with hydrofluoric acid for a durable bond [1]. A 1985 review described etched porcelain veneers as a current technique [5], and a 1993 multicentre study reported on their clinical performance [13]. A historical article in Dental Clinics of North America also surveys the technique [18].

Wikipedia adds that long-term clinical reports between 1989 and 1998, including work by Calamia, Nathanson and Strassler, and Friedman, described the reliability of bonded porcelain veneers over time.[1]

Dentists commonly remove some enamel using window, feather, bevel or incisal-overlap designs, may place temporary veneers, and then bond the final shells [1]. Temporaries, usually composite, can serve as a trial run for how the teeth look, feel and function [1]. A 2018 review emphasises keeping the preparation boundaries within enamel and covers impression-taking, provisionals, ceramic choice and surface treatment of the shell's inner side before bonding [11].

Indications listed by Wikipedia include discolored or malformed teeth, enamel hypoplasia, fluorosis, tetracycline staining, fractures, gaps, black triangles and worn teeth [1]. Multiple veneers across the upper arch are frequently used for smile makeovers [1].

Wikipedia lists veneers among tools for single fractured or discoloured teeth, smile makeovers across the upper arch, closing gaps, filling black triangles left by gum recession, evening out colour, shape and symmetry, and covering yellowed teeth that do not respond to whitening.[1] Alternatives it names include crowns, composite bonding, cosmetic contouring and orthodontics, which reshape or move teeth by different routes and with different amounts of enamel removal.[1]

Wikipedia also describes ultra-thin so-called no-prep veneers that need little or no tooth reduction, though it flags that claim as needing a better source.[1] Temporary composite veneers can be worn while the final shells are made, letting a patient test how the teeth look, feel and function before committing.[1]

Wikipedia reports that preparation may remove about 3-30% of the tooth surface depending on technique and operator, that sensitivity and decay can occur even with proper work, and that maintenance can be expensive [1]. Critics, including Canadian dentist Michael Zuk, say veneers are overused for minor issues as 'instant orthodontics'; Wikipedia labels this a contested opinion [1]. A clinician's 15-year review described patterns of veneer failure and stressed informing patients of limitations [6]. A randomized study examined the cumulative effects of successive restorative procedures on crown flexure in intact versus veneered incisors [16].

Contraindications listed include poor hygiene, uncontrolled gum disease, high cavity rate, grinding, little enamel, unrealistic expectations and large existing restorations [1]. Reported reasons for replacement include cracking, leakage, chipping, discoloration, decay, gum recession and grinding damage; Wikipedia cites a figure that after 10 years about half of veneers are displaced, need re-treatment or are no longer satisfactory, though it notes that citation looks mismatched [1]. 'Turkey teeth' and other overseas veneer packages are discussed in other entries.

A 2011 US figure of roughly $1,000 to $3,000 per tooth is cited by Wikipedia and flagged as needing an update; cost varies with dentist experience and location [1]. Wikipedia also notes the term 'Turkey teeth' for veneers obtained through dental tourism, and a claim from a commercial source that treatment in Turkey can cost up to 70% less, a figure it flags as promotional [1].

A literature review of laboratory and clinical work examined factors influencing long-term success [2]. The 2016 meta-analysis evaluated survival and complication rates for feldspathic and glass-ceramic laminates, including debonding, fracture or chipping and secondary caries [3]. The prospective trial assessed esthetics, marginal integrity, retention, fracture and patient satisfaction at 5 and 10 years, recalling 93% of restorations at 10 years [4]. Retrospective evaluations covered 6-12 years [7], and a 2018 update discusses longevity studies up to 12 years [11].

More recent trials include a 9-year split-mouth randomized trial of colour stability and marginal discoloration with light-polymerizing versus dual-polymerizing cements [14], and an 18-month randomized trial of zirconia versus lithium disilicate laminates [15]. Registered trials continue on cementation, colour stability, sectional versus full veneers, finishing of prepared surfaces and gull-wing preparation [8][9][10][19][20].

card.summary: Thin ceramic shells bonded to the front of teeth; long-lasting in follow-up studies but they usually require irreversible enamel removal.
card.note: Enamel removal is generally permanent; costs and longevity vary with dentist and case.

quick.overview:
Porcelain veneers are custom ceramic shells bonded to front teeth to change colour, shape or spacing. They are among the best-studied cosmetic dental restorations, with long-term clinical trials and meta-analyses.

Wikipedia gives lifespans of 10 to 30 years, with chipping, debonding, decay and discoloration as reasons for replacement.
quick.mechanism: A dentist usually removes some enamel, takes an impression or scan, and a lab makes the shells, which are etched and bonded to the tooth with resin cement.
quick.risks: Reported risks are sensitivity, decay, debonding and fracture; preparation can remove a meaningful part of the tooth surface, and critics argue veneers are overused. Costs are substantial.

chain: Ceramic shell is made to a chosen shade and shape
Bonded to the front of the tooth after enamel preparation
Colour, shape, length and gaps change at once
A whiter, more uniform, better-proportioned smile
angle.text: Veneers change what teeth look like in a matter of visits. They are used for stained, chipped, worn or gapped teeth, and for full-arch smile makeovers.
